summary: Describes IS-IS extensions for Traffic Engineering, adding information to link state PDUs about network state for TE calculations. It is informational. It was updated by RFC 4205 and replaced by RFC 5305.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS is the routing protocol that many large networks use to work out the best path between two places. It normally knows only a cost for each link. This RFC lets a router also publish how much bandwidth a link has, how much of it is already spoken for, and which group the link belongs to. Those extra details are what a traffic engineer needs to plan a path for a particular stream of traffic.

what is the up/down bit in is-is
subtitle: Extra IS-IS link state information so routers can compute explicit paths, not just shortest ones.

tldr.problem: A shortest path calculation needs one number per link, the cost. Traffic engineering needs more: link bandwidth, reserved bandwidth and an administrative group for each link. The original IS-IS TLVs carried none of that, and the metric was limited to 63.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new TLV types: an extended IS reachability TLV that carries a 24-bit metric and nested sub-TLVs about the link, an extended IP reachability TLV with a 32-bit metric and an up/down bit, and a TLV holding a stable 4-octet router ID.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3784 is an Informational document from June 2004. It has been obsoleted by RFC 5305 and updated by RFC 4205, which revised the same extensions.

today: RFC 3784 is an Informational document from June 2004, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 5305 and updated by RFC 4205. The RFC says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and that it does not discuss the mechanisms and procedures for migrating to the new TLVs.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Needed Traffic Engineering Information
sections.content:
IS-IS is specified in ISO 10589, with IPv4 extensions in RFC 1195. Each router advertises one or more Link State Protocol Data Units, and each LSP holds a fixed header followed by a series of tuples made of a Type, a Length and a Value. These tuples are called TLVs, and they let a protocol carry new pieces of information without changing its overall shape.

The gap this RFC fills is that a shortest path calculation needs one number per link, the cost. Traffic engineering, which builds explicit paths for particular flows, needs more: the bandwidth a link can carry, how much of it is already reserved, and the administrative group, or colour, that the link belongs to. The original TLVs carried none of that.

The RFC therefore replaces the IS neighbour TLV and the IP reachability TLV with extended versions that carry a wider metric and a set of sub-TLVs holding the extra detail. A secondary goal is to widen the range of the IS-IS metric. It also notes that the router ID is useful for traffic engineering because it gives one stable address that can always be used to name a router. The document says nothing about the mechanisms and procedures for migrating to the new TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS is a link state routing protocol: every router tells its neighbours about the links it has, and each router then works out the cheapest path. To plan a path for a specific flow, a network operator also needs to know how much capacity each link has. This RFC adds that information to the messages IS-IS already sends.

sections.title: Sub-TLVs Inside TLVs
sections.content:
A sub-TLV is a tuple nested inside another TLV. A TLV carries extra information in an IS-IS packet; a sub-TLV carries extra information about one particular TLV. Each sub-TLV has a one-octet Type field, a one-octet Length field and zero or more octets of Value. The Type says what the value holds and the Length gives the size of that value in octets, so a sub-TLV can hold several items of a known size, and the number of items can be worked out from the length of the whole sub-TLV.

A receiver that meets a sub-TLV it does not recognize must ignore it and skip to the next one. That is what makes the scheme extensible: a router that predates a sub-TLV type can still read the rest of the LSP.

The sub-TLV type space is managed by the IETF IS-IS working group, with new values allocated after review on the group's mailing list and after a document describing the use of the value has been published. If the working group has been disbanded, the review is done by a Designated Expert assigned by the responsible Area Director.
sections.plainLanguage: A sub-TLV is a small labelled box inside a larger labelled box. The outer one describes a link or a prefix, and the inner ones add details about that particular link or prefix. A router that does not understand one of the inner boxes skips it and carries on reading.

sections.title: The Extended IS Reachability TLV
sections.content:
The existing IS reachability TLV, type 2 from ISO 10589, lists the IS neighbours of the advertising router. For each neighbour it holds a default metric, a delay, a monetary cost, a reliability and the 7-octet ID of the neighbour. Only the default metric is commonly used, and the other three are unused overhead. The metric was one octet: one bit for internal or external, and one bit that RFC 2966 later defined as the up/down bit, leaving 6 bits for the value and a range of 0 to 63.

Type 22 replaces that structure. Each neighbour is now 7 octets of system ID and pseudonode number, 3 octets of metric, 1 octet giving the length of the sub-TLVs, and 0 to 244 octets of sub-TLVs. The metric is encoded as a 24-bit unsigned integer. The neighbour field is still 7 octets, so an entry still costs 11 octets and one TLV can still hold 23 neighbours.

The RFC sets MAX_PATH_METRIC to 4,261,412,864 (0xFE000000, which is 232 minus 225), and any metric at or above that value counts as exactly that value. A link advertised with the maximum link metric, 2^24 - 1, must not be used in the normal shortest-path computation. That lets a router advertise a link that is available for traffic engineering but not for hop-by-hop routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The new TLV type 22 describes one neighbouring router per entry, using the same 11 octets as the old type 2 did. Three of those octets now hold the cost of the link, so the cost can be far larger than 63, and the rest of the entry can carry sub-TLVs about the link's capacity and colour.

sections.title: The Extended IP Reachability TLV and the Up/Down Bit
sections.content:
The existing IP reachability TLVs, types 128 and 130, carry IPv4 prefixes in a similar shape and also limit the default metric to 0 to 63. They have a second gap: RFC 1195 lets a router advertise prefixes upward in the level hierarchy, but defines no way to advertise them downward.

Type 135 fixes both. Each entry has 4 octets of metric information, 1 octet of control information made of an up/down bit, a bit saying whether sub-TLVs are present and 6 bits of prefix length, then 0 to 4 octets of IPv4 prefix, then optional sub-TLVs. The 6 bits of prefix length hold values from 0 to 32, and the prefix is written in the fewest octets possible for that many significant bits; the remaining bits are sent as zero and ignored on receipt. A prefix with a metric above MAX_PATH_METRIC must be left out of the normal shortest-path computation, so a prefix can be advertised for purposes other than the ordinary routing table.

The up/down bit stops prefixes from looping between levels. Without it, a router that learns a prefix at level 2 could advertise it down into a level 1 area, and another router could send it back up, leaving a forwarding loop that runs partly through level 1 and partly through level 2. The bit is set to 0 when a prefix first enters IS-IS, set to 1 when the prefix travels down the hierarchy, and a prefix with the bit set may only be advertised further down. A prefix advertised between two areas at the same level also gets the bit set to 1. Keeping prefixes moving along the hierarchy is what stops the information from looping.
sections.plainLanguage: The extended IP reachability TLV type 135 lists the address prefixes a router is reachable for, with a much larger cost value than before. It also adds one bit that records whether a prefix has already travelled down the IS-IS hierarchy. A router refuses to send a prefix back up once it has come down, which is what prevents two routers from passing the same prefix back and forth and creating a routing loop.

sections.title: The Traffic Engineering Router ID TLV
sections.content:
The Traffic Engineering router ID TLV, type 134, carries the 4-octet router ID of the router that originated the LSP. For traffic engineering this gives one stable address that a path can refer to from several hops away, whatever state the router's interfaces are in. It also lets traffic engineering map between the IS-IS topology and the OSPF topology when both run in the same domain.

A router that does not implement traffic engineering may include or omit the TLV; one that does implement it must include it, and it should appear at most once in an LSP. If the router advertises prefixes over BGP with the BGP router ID as the next hop, the Traffic Engineering router ID should be the same value.

The RFC also forbids a router from installing a /32 prefix for the router ID in its forwarding table, because a router that does not support the TLV would not know about that route and traffic could loop. The same prohibition applies to the IPv4 interface address and neighbour address sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: TLV type 134 simply names the router that sent the LSP, using a fixed four-octet address. Traffic engineers use that name when they build a path, because it stays valid however the router's interfaces are configured. Routers must not turn that name into a route of its own, since a router that does not read the TLV would then have a forwarding loop.

sections.title: Registered TLV and Sub-TLV Numbers
sections.content:
Three new IS-IS TLV types are defined and reflected in the IS-IS TLV code point registry: 22 for the extended IS reachability TLV, 134 for the Traffic Engineering router ID TLV and 135 for the extended IP reachability TLV. All three are carried in LSPs only.

Two new registries are created. The first covers sub-TLVs of TLV 22 over the range 0 to 255, and is initialized with the seven sub-TLVs this RFC defines: 3 administrative group, 6 IPv4 interface address, 8 IPv4 neighbour address, 9 maximum link bandwidth, 10 reservable link bandwidth, 11 unreserved bandwidth and 18 TE default metric. Values 250 to 254 are reserved for Cisco-specific extensions and 255 is reserved for future expansion. The second registry covers sub-TLVs of TLV 135 over the same range, and this RFC defines none of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers the numbers other equipment will look for: TLV types 22, 134 and 135, and the sub-TLV numbers inside type 22. Values from 250 to 254 are set aside for Cisco extensions and 255 is held back for later.

viz.caption: THE FIXED PART OF ONE NEIGHBOUR ENTRY (RFC 3784)

fields.name: System ID and pseudonode number
fields.desc: Seven octets identifying the neighbour: its system ID, typically 6 octets, plus one octet for the pseudonode number.

fields.name: Default metric
fields.desc: The cost of the link, as a 24-bit unsigned integer. The old one-octet metric allowed only 0 to 63.

fields.name: Sub-TLV length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the sub-TLVs that follow for this neighbour.

viz.caption: SUB-TLVS OF THE EXTENDED IS REACHABILITY TLV (RFC 3784)

items.label: Administrative group
items.desc: A 4-octet bit mask set by the administrator. Each set bit is one administrative group on the interface.

items.label: IPv4 interface address
items.desc: A 4-octet IPv4 address for the interface described by the main TLV.

items.label: IPv4 neighbor address
items.desc: A 4-octet IPv4 address of a neighbouring router on this link.

items.label: Maximum link bandwidth
items.desc: The most bandwidth usable on this link in this direction, as a 32-bit IEEE floating point value in bytes per second.

items.label: Reservable link bandwidth
items.desc: The most bandwidth that can be reserved in this direction, as a 32-bit IEEE floating point value in bytes per second.

items.label: Unreserved bandwidth
items.desc: Eight 32-bit IEEE floating point values, one for each setup priority from 0 to 7, in bytes per second.

items.label: TE default metric
items.desc: A 24-bit unsigned integer, administratively assigned, used to present a differently weighted topology to traffic engineering.
